# RV power station and solar picks

No single combo fits every RV, so I've matched picks to how you travel. I can only link to the review pages and one merchant page from my search results, not each manufacturer's own page. The review pages have price buttons.

## 1. Full-time or boondocking, running the roof AC: EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3
- It has 4,096Wh, 4,000W continuous and 8,000W surge, and it expands past 12kWh.
- A 13,500 BTU roof AC draws about 1,500W running and spikes above 3,000W at startup. This unit handles that easily.
- It recharges 0-80% in about 50 minutes from a wall outlet.
- It's heavy, so moving it is a two-person job, and it's the priciest option once you add batteries.
- Check price: [EmergencyEnergy RV comparison](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/)

## 2. Best mid-range value with a built-in RV outlet: BLUETTI AC200L
- It has 2,048Wh, 2,400W output, a 30A RV port and up to 1,200W of solar input. It weighs about 62 lb.
- That solar ceiling lets a large rooftop or ground array actually deliver its full output.
- Check price: [Smart Energy Edge camping guide](https://smartenergyedge.com/best-portable-power-station-with-solar-panels-for-camping/)
- One source lists the older AC200P with only a 700W solar limit, so make sure you buy the AC200L.

## 3. Weekend trips with a fridge, laptop and Starlink: EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus
- It has 1,024Wh, 1,800W output and a 1,000W solar input across two 500W ports. It weighs about 28 lb.
- It expands up to 5kWh.
- Check price: [Smart Energy Edge camping guide](https://smartenergyedge.com/best-portable-power-station-with-solar-panels-for-camping/)
- For a lighter, simpler option, the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 (1,070Wh, about 24 lb) is easy to use but caps solar at 400W. It's covered in the same guide.

## 4. Big capacity for the money: ALLPOWERS R4000
- It has 3,456Wh, 3,600W at 120V, an RV outlet, up to 2,000W solar input and a 5-year warranty.
- It's listed at $1,499, and the site reports codes that bring it to about $1,319 (EXTRA12) or $1,349 (ALLPOWERS26 or EXTRA10). Codes expire in November and December 2026, and checkout has the final word.
- It weighs 45 kg (about 99 lb), so it's more of a stay-put unit. To reach 2,000W of solar you need panels on all three inputs.
- [Buy at ALLPOWERS (affiliate link)](https://dealectric.com/go/allpowers-r4000-3456wh). The listing is from a deal site that earns a commission.

## Solar panels
- **Check the station's solar input limit first.** Panels beyond it add nothing.
- Bundled panel wattage varies by package, so confirm what's included.
- For weekend use, a 200W foldable suitcase panel is a common pairing. NomadSignal suggests the Renogy 200W Foldable Solar Suitcase ([guide](https://nomadsignal.co/blogs/news/jackery-vs-ecoflow-vs-bluetti-vanlife)).
- For a 2kWh unit, plan on 300-400W or more to refill it in a day of good sun ([EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/)).

## Quick sizing
- **Weekend trips, no AC:** about 1,000Wh.
- **Multi-day off-grid:** 2,000Wh or more.
- **Roof AC:** 3,000W or more of output, or a soft-start kit.

I couldn't verify current prices. Prices and specs change, so confirm on the retailer's page. The EmergencyEnergy article is written for Ontario, so ignore its Canadian electrical rules. The general advice still applies. Hardwiring anything into your RV is best left to a licensed electrician.

Tell me your RV type, whether you run a roof AC, and your budget, and I can narrow this to one pick.
